definition: An approach to building software in short cycles, delivering working software often and adjusting to feedback instead of following a fixed up-front plan. The term comes from the 2001 Agile Manifesto.
example: A team that releases a usable slice every two weeks and changes its plan after each user demo is working in an Agile way.

definition: A one-page statement written in 2001 by seventeen practitioners in Snowbird, Utah. It sets out four values, such as working software over comprehensive documentation, while saying the items on the right still have value.

A sequential way of running a project: gather all requirements, then design, build, test and release, each phase finishing before the next starts. Problems with the requirements tend to surface late, when changes are most expensive.

A lightweight framework for teams working in fixed-length iterations called Sprints, with three accountabilities, five events and three artefacts. Its official definition is the Scrum Guide by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland.
The short official definition of Scrum by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, last revised in November 2020. Many common practices, such as story points, are not part of it.
A fixed-length iteration of one month or less in which a Scrum Team turns Product Backlog items into a usable Increment. A new Sprint starts immediately after the previous one ends.
A small group, typically 10 or fewer people, made up of one Product Owner, one Scrum Master and the Developers. It has no sub-teams or hierarchy.
The Scrum accountability for maximising the value of the product. The Product Owner owns and orders the Product Backlog.
The Scrum accountability for helping the team and organisation use Scrum effectively, including getting impediments removed. It is not a project-manager role.
The Scrum event that starts a Sprint: the team decides why the Sprint is valuable (the Sprint Goal), what can be done and how. It is timeboxed to at most 8 hours for a one-month Sprint.
A 15-minute Scrum event each working day where the Developers inspect progress towards the Sprint Goal and adapt their plan.
The Scrum event near the end of a Sprint where the team and stakeholders inspect what was done and decide what to do next. It is a working session, timeboxed to 4 hours for a one-month Sprint.
The Scrum event that ends a Sprint, where the team looks at how it works (people, process, tools) and picks improvements. It is timeboxed to 3 hours for a one-month Sprint.
The single objective for a Sprint, set during Sprint Planning. It is the commitment attached to the Sprint Backlog and gives the team flexibility over exactly which work delivers it.
The long-term objective for the product that the Scrum Team plans against. It is the commitment attached to the Product Backlog.
An ordered list of the work that might be done to improve a product; in Scrum the Product Owner owns and orders it. Outside Scrum, a backlog is any prioritised list of work waiting to be done.
The Sprint Goal, the Product Backlog items selected for the Sprint and the plan for delivering them. The Developers own it and update it as they learn.
A usable piece of progress towards the Product Goal that meets the Definition of Done. Several Increments may be made in one Sprint.
A shared, explicit description of the quality an Increment must meet, for example tested, reviewed and documented. Work that does not meet it is not part of the Increment.
A fixed maximum length of time for an activity or event. When the time is up, the activity ends, whether or not everything was covered.
example: A one-month Sprint's Retrospective is timeboxed to 3 hours.

definition: The idea, central to Scrum, that knowledge comes from experience and decisions should be based on what is observed. Scrum puts it into practice through transparency, inspection and adaptation.
The ongoing activity of breaking down, clarifying and sizing Product Backlog items so they are ready to work on. It is not one of the five Scrum events.
A short description of a feature from a user's point of view, often in the form 'As a <role>, I want <goal> so that <benefit>'. It is a common practice, not part of Scrum itself.
A chart of the work remaining (for example story points) against time, used to see whether a team is on track to finish a Sprint or release.

A method for managing knowledge work by visualising it on a board with a column per stage, limiting work in progress and improving flow. David J. Anderson adapted it for software from Toyota's production system in the mid-2000s.
Toyota's manufacturing approach, in which kanban cards ('signboards') signalled when to produce more parts. It inspired Lean and Kanban in software.
Work in progress: items that have been started but not finished. Too much WIP slows everything down, because items queue and people switch between tasks.
An explicit maximum number of items allowed in a stage of a workflow (or the whole board) at once. When a stage is full, nobody starts new work there until something moves on.
example: A Review column with a WIP limit of 2 accepts a third card only after one leaves.

definition: A way of moving work in which a stage takes new work only when it has capacity, instead of upstream stages pushing work onto it. It is the basis of Kanban.

A result from queueing theory, proved by John Little in 1961: in a stable system, the average number of items in it equals the average arrival (or finishing) rate times the average time each item spends inside.
example: With 12 items in progress and 4 finished a week, each item takes 3 weeks on average.

definition: The mathematical study of waiting lines: how arrivals, service times and capacity determine queue lengths and waiting times.
How long one work item takes from the moment work on it starts until it is finished. Kanban teams track it to see how quickly work flows.
The time from a request (or a code change) entering a process until it is delivered. In software delivery metrics, lead time for changes is the time from commit to running in production.
How long an unfinished item has been in progress so far. Old items on a Kanban board are a warning that work is stuck.

A picture of how the possible range of a project estimate is wide early on and narrows as decisions are made. Steve McConnell's version illustrates an early range of 0.25× to 4× the eventual outcome; it is a model, not a statistical law.
The tendency, described by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky in 1979, to underestimate how long one's own tasks will take, even when similar tasks have overrun before.
Douglas Hofstadter's joke rule: 'It always takes longer than you expect, even when you take into account Hofstadter's law.' It captures how persistent underestimation is.
Sizing work by comparing it with other work ('about twice the password-reset page') rather than in hours. People tend to compare sizes more consistently than they predict absolute durations.

A unit for relative estimation: a number expressing how big a piece of work is compared with a reference item, combining effort, complexity and uncertainty. Points are only meaningful inside the team that assigned them.
An estimation scale such as 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 whose gaps grow, roughly following the Fibonacci sequence. The widening gaps reflect that bigger items are more uncertain.

An estimation technique in which everyone picks a card with their estimate and all reveal at once, then the high and low estimators explain their reasoning. Revealing together reduces anchoring on the first number spoken.
The tendency for an estimate to be pulled towards the first number a person hears, even when that number is arbitrary.

The number of story points a team completes per Sprint, usually averaged over recent Sprints and used to forecast what it can take on. It is a planning tool for one team, not a productivity score to compare teams.
example: A team averaging 21 points a Sprint with 105 points left needs roughly 5 more Sprints.

definition: An estimate given as three values for one task: optimistic, most likely and pessimistic. It shows the uncertainty that a single number hides.

Program Evaluation and Review Technique, a planning method developed for the US Navy's Polaris programme in the late 1950s. Its estimate formula weights a task's most likely duration four times as heavily as the optimistic and pessimistic ones, then divides by six.
example: Optimistic 2, most likely 4 and pessimistic 12 days give (2 + 16 + 12) / 6 = 5 days.

definition: A family of probability distributions for a quantity that lies between a fixed minimum and maximum, which can be lopsided. PERT's weighting comes from approximating task durations with one.
A way to forecast by running a random model thousands of times and looking at the spread of results. In delivery forecasting, each run samples past weekly throughput until the backlog is finished.
example: Sampling 10,000 futures from 8 past weeks can show a 50% chance of finishing within 11 weeks and 85% within 13.

definition: Drawing random values, with replacement, from data you already have to simulate possible futures or estimate uncertainty. It assumes the past data is representative.
The value below which a given percentage of observations fall. The 99th percentile (p99) of latency is the time that roughly 99% of requests beat, so about 1% are slower.
example: If p99 is 300 ms, about 1 request in 100 takes longer than 300 ms.

definition: The middle value of a set of numbers once sorted: half are below it and half above. It is the 50th percentile and, unlike the mean, is not dragged around by a few extreme values.
A movement that avoids estimating individual items: work is split into small, similar-sized pieces and delivery is forecast from measured throughput.
Fred Brooks's 1975 observation that 'adding manpower to a late software project makes it later', because newcomers need training and coordination costs rise.
Fred Brooks's 1975 book of essays on software project management, drawn from his experience leading IBM's OS/360. It is the source of Brooks's law.
Copying the visible rituals of a practice (meetings, boards, ceremonies) without the feedback and adaptation that make it work.
Observing, forming a hypothesis, predicting what else must be true, testing the prediction and drawing a conclusion. Methodical debugging follows the same loop.
A description of a defect: what happened, what was expected, the exact steps, inputs, versions, environment and time. A precise one makes the bug far easier to reproduce.
The smallest, fastest set of steps or input that still triggers a bug, ideally as an automated failing test. It makes the cause easier to see and becomes a regression test.

Andreas Zeller's systematic method for shrinking a failing input: remove chunks and keep any smaller input that still fails, splitting into finer chunks when no removal works. Its ddmin algorithm produces a 1-minimal input.
An input from which removing any single remaining piece makes the failure disappear. It is minimal locally, not necessarily the smallest possible failing input.
A mode of git bisect that runs a script on each candidate commit and uses its exit code to mark it: 0 good, 1 to 127 except 125 bad, 125 skip, and above 127 aborts the search.
The number a program returns to its caller when it finishes. By convention 0 means success and other values mean some kind of failure.
Finding a bug by adding output statements that show values as the program runs. It is quick and works everywhere, but must be removed or turned into proper logging.

Recording events and values from a running program to a file or service, with timestamps and levels such as INFO or ERROR. Structured logs use key-value fields so they can be searched and correlated, for example by request ID.
Python's built-in function that returns an unambiguous text form of a value, so '1' (a string) prints with quotes and 1 (a number) without.
A tool that can pause a running program, step through it line by line and inspect or change variables, without editing the code.
Python's built-in command-line debugger. Commands such as n (next), s (step into), c (continue) and p (print) control it; breakpoint() drops into it.
A marked place in the code where a debugger pauses the program so you can inspect its state. In Python 3.7+, calling breakpoint() starts the debugger there.
A breakpoint that pauses only when an expression is true, such as n == 0, so a debugger stops on the one bad iteration out of thousands.

Debugger commands for moving through code: step over runs the current line, including any calls, and stops at the next one; step into enters the function being called; step out runs until the current function returns.
Inspecting a program in a debugger after it has crashed, landing in the frame that raised the exception with its variables intact. In Python, python -m pdb or pdb.pm() does this.
Read-eval-print loop: an interactive prompt, such as Python's >>>, that runs each line as you type it and prints the result.
A bug that changes or disappears when you try to observe it, typically because adding prints or a debugger alters timing. Race conditions are the classic cause.
A bug that fails reliably under the same conditions, the opposite of a heisenbug.
Memory that a C or C++ program reads before writing a value to it, so it holds whatever was there before. Reading it gives unpredictable results.
A compiler-based tool for C, C++ and Go that detects data races at run time in the code paths a program actually executes.
A compiler-based tool that detects classes of memory-safety errors, such as buffer overflows and use after free, in executed code.
A compiler feature that adds run-time checks to a program to catch a class of bugs, such as data races or invalid memory access. It finds bugs only on paths that run.
A tool that watches memory accesses from different threads and reports data races. Go has one built in through the -race flag.
Protection against bugs in how a program reads and writes memory, such as reading past the end of a buffer or using memory after freeing it.
A file recording the exact version of every dependency a project installed, such as poetry.lock or package-lock.json, so every environment gets identical versions.
A set of regional settings, such as language, number format and currency, that changes how a program formats or parses text. 1,5 means one and a half in a German locale.

Whether upper- and lower-case letters count as different. A case-sensitive file system treats Report.txt and report.txt as two different files; Linux file systems usually are, while macOS's default file system is case-insensitive.
Following one request across several services by tagging it with a shared trace ID and recording a timed span for each step, so you can see where its time went.
Changing several things at once, more or less at random, until a bug seems to go away. You learn nothing about the cause and may add new bugs.
Explaining a problem line by line to someone else, or even to a rubber duck, which forces you to state your assumptions and often exposes the wrong one.
A change that moves or transforms stored data or the database structure, such as adding a column and copying values into it.
A tool that measures where a program spends its time or memory, function by function, so you optimise the part that actually matters.
Making code faster, usually at the cost of clarity, before measurement shows that part matters. Knuth's 1974 line calls it 'the root of all evil' for about 97% of small efficiencies.

Gene Amdahl's 1967 formula for the overall speedup from improving one part of a program: the untouched part limits the gain. Speeding up 30% of the runtime infinitely gives at most about 1.43 times overall.
The ratio of old running time to new running time. A speedup of 2 means the work now takes half as long.
The slowest few per cent of response times, measured by high percentiles such as p99. A good average can hide a bad tail, and users who make many requests are likely to hit it.
A repeatable measurement of how long something takes (or how much it uses), so different versions can be compared under the same conditions.
A benchmark of a tiny piece of code, such as one function or expression, run many times. It is precise but may say little about a whole request.
Python's standard module for timing small snippets: it runs the code many times and handles timer details. Its docs suggest taking the minimum of repeated runs.
Running code for a while before measuring, so caches are filled, imports and connections are done and any JIT compiler has optimised it.
The first run of code or a service before caches, connections and compiled code are ready, which is usually slower than later runs.
An alternative Python implementation with a just-in-time compiler, often much faster than the standard CPython for long-running pure-Python code.
Google's JavaScript engine, used in Chrome and Node.js, which compiles JavaScript to machine code with a JIT compiler.
A processor deliberately slowing its clock to stay within temperature or power limits, which makes timings on laptops noisy.
A profiler that hooks every function call and return and counts them exactly, at the cost of overhead that hits tiny functions hardest. cProfile is one.
A profiler that records the program's call stack at regular intervals and estimates where time goes from how often each function appears. It is approximate but usually low-overhead.
Python's built-in deterministic profiler. It reports, per function, the number of calls (ncalls), time in the function itself (tottime) and time including callees (cumtime).
A sampling profiler for Python that runs as a separate process and can attach to a running program by PID without restarting it. It can draw flame graphs.
Linux's built-in performance analysis tool, which can sample call stacks and read hardware counters for any process.
Process identifier: the number an operating system gives each running process. Tools use it to attach to a specific process.
The cProfile column giving how many times a function was called. A high count alone does not mean a function is expensive.
The cProfile column giving the time spent inside a function itself, excluding the functions it called (its self time).
The cProfile column giving the time spent in a function including everything it called. The top-level function's cumtime is close to the whole runtime.
Time spent executing a function's own code, not the functions it calls. In cProfile this is tottime; in a flame graph, the exposed top of a box.
Fetching a list with one database query and then running one more query for each item in it, so N items cost N + 1 round trips. Joining or batching usually cuts it to one or two queries.
example: Listing 300 orders with each customer's name can cost 301 queries.

definition: Combining many small operations into one larger one, such as one query for 5,000 rows instead of 5,000 queries, to pay fixed per-call costs once.
Brendan Gregg's visualisation of sampled call stacks: each box is a function, boxes above are its callees, and width shows the share of samples. The x-axis is not time.
A call-stack picture like a flame graph but with time along the x-axis, so you can see when each function ran.
Walking back through a thread's call stack to list which function called which. Profilers need it to record full stacks.
Time a thread spends not running on a CPU: waiting for I/O, locks, timers or its turn to be scheduled. A CPU-only profiler cannot see it.
The time a CPU actually spent executing a process's instructions. It excludes time spent waiting.
How the operating system decides which ready (runnable) thread runs on each CPU next. A runnable thread may still wait for its turn.
A database log of queries that took longer than a set threshold, used to find expensive queries.
Brendan Gregg's checklist for system performance: for every resource (CPU, memory, disk, network) check Utilisation, Saturation (queued work) and Errors.
The fraction of time a resource is busy, or the share of its capacity in use.
Describes work whose speed is limited by waiting for input/output such as disks or networks, rather than by computation (CPU-bound). Overlapping the waits helps I/O-bound work.
Structuring a program so several tasks are in progress at once, for example with threads or asyncio, so one task's waiting can overlap another's work.
A Python library for fast numerical arrays; operations on whole arrays run in compiled code.
Replacing an element-by-element loop with one operation over a whole array, which runs in optimised compiled code.
A small local tweak, such as caching an attribute lookup in a local variable, that saves tiny amounts of time. Worth doing only in a proven hot loop.
A loop where a program spends a large share of its running time, so small improvements there matter.
Resident set size: how much of a process's memory is currently held in physical RAM.
An operating system moving memory pages to disk when RAM runs short, which makes programs dramatically slower.
Out of memory: the Linux kernel's mechanism that kills a process when the system or a container runs out of memory.
Python's standard module for tracing memory allocations. Comparing two snapshots shows which lines allocated the memory that grew.
A tool that records what is allocated on a program's heap and where, to find memory growth.
Objects that refer to each other in a loop. Python's cycle collector normally frees them once nothing else refers to them.
An automated test that fails if code becomes slower or uses more resources than a threshold, catching performance regressions.
A load-testing flaw where the generator waits for each response before sending the next, so it sends fewer requests during a stall and under-reports slow responses.
An HTTP load generator that sends requests at a constant rate and measures latency from each intended send time, avoiding coordinated omission.
A load generator that sends a new request only after the previous one finishes. An open-loop one sends at a fixed rate regardless of responses, as independent users do.
A Unix command that runs another command with administrator (root) privileges.
A Django model field linking each row to one row of another table, for example each order to its customer.
One request sent and its response received. Each round trip pays network and processing overhead.
A set of reusable open database connections. When all are busy, new requests wait for one.
A compiled systems programming language that aims for C-like speed with memory safety.
A unit of data: 1,000,000 bytes in SI usage, though some software means 1,048,576 bytes.
A unit of data: 1,000,000,000 bytes in SI usage (some software means 1,073,741,824 bytes).
The SI base unit of mass.
Kent Beck's image for keeping refactoring and feature work apart: wear one hat to add behaviour, the other to restructure, and never both at once.
What callers, users or other systems can see a piece of code do: its outputs, errors, side effects and public formats. Refactoring, like a compiler optimisation, must leave it unchanged.
Refactoring just before adding a feature, to reshape the code so the feature fits naturally.
Renaming and extracting while reading confusing code until it makes sense, so the next reader gets your understanding for free.
Making small improvements to code as you pass through it while doing other work.
The habit of leaving code a little better than you found it each time you touch it.
A dedicated, scheduled chunk of refactoring work for an area that neglect has made painful. Healthy teams need less of it.
A Git command that discards uncommitted changes to the named files, putting them back to their last committed state.
A group of values, such as start and end dates, that always travel together through many functions. Bundling them into one object is the usual fix.
A code smell: a function long enough that it is hard to understand at once. Extract Function is the usual fix.
The refactoring that moves a coherent piece of code into its own named function, so the name documents its intent.
The reverse of extracting: replacing calls to a function, or uses of a variable, with its body or value when the indirection no longer helps.
The refactoring that gives a complicated expression a name by assigning it to a well-named variable.
The refactoring that moves a function next to the data it uses most, the usual fix for feature envy.
The refactoring that replaces a group of parameters always passed together with one object, such as a DateRange.
The refactoring that replaces a branch on type, repeated in several places, with one class per case that each implement the behaviour.
The refactoring that wraps a bare value such as a string phone number in a small class with its own behaviour.
The refactoring that splits a function which both returns a value and changes state into one that only reads and one that only changes.
A background program that understands a programming language and gives editors features such as go-to-definition and automated rename.
JetBrains' IDE, mainly for Java and Kotlin, with extensive automated refactorings.
JetBrains' IDE for Python.
Microsoft's free code editor, extended through plugins and language servers.
Python's built-in function that looks up an attribute by a name held in a string, which automated refactoring tools cannot always follow.
An interface placed in front of a component so callers depend on the interface, not the implementation behind it.
A branch that stays separate from the main branch for weeks or months, drifting from it and ending in a painful merge.
Sending copies of real requests to a new implementation and comparing its answers with the old one, without using the new answers. Writes and side effects must be suppressed.
A rounding rule in which a value exactly halfway rounds up, so 10.005 becomes 10.01; truncation would just cut it to 10.00.
The number of people who would have to disappear before a project stalls. A bus factor of one is a single point of failure.
One part, or one person, whose failure stops the whole system.
A short document written before building something substantial, setting out context, goals and non-goals, the design and the alternatives considered, so reviewers can catch expensive mistakes early.
Something a design doc explicitly says the project will not do. Listing non-goals stops scope creep and endless debate.
The design-doc section listing the other designs examined and why they lost, often the most valuable part for future readers.
The gradual, uncontrolled growth of what a project is expected to deliver.
Keeping documentation in the same repository as the code, in plain text, reviewed and updated in the same pull requests.
Step-by-step instructions for an operational task or alert: what it means, how to check impact and what to try first.
Being responsible for responding to alerts from production systems during a shift, often out of hours. Google's SRE book caps it at about 25% of an engineer's time.
The device or app that alerts an on-call engineer. To page someone is to send an alert that needs their urgent attention.
Google's discipline of running production systems with software engineering. The SRE book (2016) describes its practices.
The agreed route for getting more help when an on-call engineer cannot handle a problem alone.
An on-call rotation split across time zones so each site covers its daytime hours, avoiding night shifts.
Passing responsibility to the next on-call engineer with notes on what fired, what is open and what to watch.
An automatic notification that a system needs attention. Alerts that wake someone should be urgent and actionable.
Becoming desensitised to alerts because most are noise, so a real one is missed.
Alerting on what users experience, such as errors or slow responses, rather than on internal causes like high CPU.
A service that keeps no client data between requests, so any instance can handle any request.
Service-level objective: a target for how reliable a service should be, such as 99.9% of requests succeeding over 30 days.
The amount of unreliability an SLO allows, such as 0.1% of requests; when it is spent, teams slow releases.
The organised process for handling a production outage: assessing severity, coordinating responders and restoring service.
A ranking of how serious an incident is, which sets how urgently and widely the response happens.
A written review after a significant incident covering impact, timeline, contributing factors and follow-up actions with owners.
Reviewing failures on the assumption that people acted reasonably given what they knew, and fixing the system that made the mistake easy rather than punishing people.
A follow-up task from a postmortem or meeting, with an owner and due date, tracked like other work.
One of the several conditions that together caused an incident. Real incidents rarely have a single root cause.
A shared belief in a team that it is safe to admit mistakes and take interpersonal risks. Amy Edmondson's research linked it with team learning.
Google's internal study of what makes teams effective, which reported psychological safety as the most important of five factors.
Getting a new team member productive: access, context, codebase and practices.
The whole team working on the same thing at the same time on one screen.
Communicating through written proposals, documents and threads that people answer in their own time, rather than meetings.
Celebrating individuals who rescue crises, which rewards the concentrated knowledge that causes them.
Which people or teams are responsible for a component. Rotating ownership spreads knowledge.
Something a business does to create value, such as payments or catalogue, often used to draw team and service boundaries.
Storing every change to application state as an event in an append-only log and rebuilding current state from those events.
A page of live charts and figures showing a system's health.
A tracked work item in an issue tracker such as Jira.
The extra cost future changes pay because code is not in the shape you now know it should be. Ward Cunningham coined the metaphor in 1992.
The one-off work needed to bring code up to the design you now want.
The extra effort every future change costs because the debt has not been repaid. Interest equals extra time per change times how often the code changes.
example: 2 extra days × 8 changes a quarter = 16 days a quarter.

definition: A portfolio-management product whose 1992 experience report by Ward Cunningham introduced the technical debt metaphor.
Martin Fowler's sorting of debt by whether it was deliberate or inadvertent and prudent or reckless; each corner needs a different response.
Debt from letting libraries and frameworks fall behind their current versions.
Debt from understanding concentrated in too few people.
Debt from missing, slow or flaky tests.
When a vendor stops support, including security fixes. Python 2 reached end of life on 1 January 2020.
An identifier in the public catalogue of security vulnerabilities, such as CVE-2021-44228.
A weakness that an attacker could exploit.
The older major version of Python, incompatible in places with Python 3.
How often a file or module is modified, taken from version-control history.
A crude size measure: the number of lines in a file or function.
How long an investment takes to earn back its cost. For a debt fix: fix cost ÷ interest saved per period.
example: A 20-day fix saving 16 days a quarter pays back in 1.25 quarters.

definition: A fixed share of each iteration set aside for debt or maintenance.
Knowledge held by one person or group and not shared.
In Fowler's design stamina hypothesis, the point after which a team with good internal design delivers more than a team that neglected it.
Releasing a change to a small share of users first, widening it only if healthy.
